To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
patients’ and spouses’ negative appraisals were associated with worse QOL, and that patients’ and their partners’ perceived dyadic communication was associated with better QOL.

appraisals of prostate cancer illness and perceived dyadic communication are associated with quality of life among prostate cancer patients and their spouses, and that the associations between perceived dyadic communication and quality of life are mediated by appraisals of disease.

(1) spouses with more negative illness appraisals at the start of treatment perceived worse dyadic relationship 4 months later and worse quality of life 8 months later, and patients with more positive appraisals of their illness perceived better dyadic relationship 2 months later and better quality of life 4 months later; (2) patients and spouses who perceived better dyadic communication at the start of the second year after treatment had better quality of life at the end of the second year;
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between patients’ and their spouse’s appraisals of prostate cancer, perceived dyadic (couple) communication and QOL.
the interdependent relationships among patients’ and spouses’ perceptions of their illness and their quality of life, and the mediating role of their perceived dyadic communications.
the interdependent relationships that exist between patients’ and their partners’ appraisals and QOL over time and whether their perceived dyadic communications mediated these relationships.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results from the study suggest that the patient and the spouse have a mutual effect on their own quality of life and that the quality of dyadic communication mediates these relationships.
the appraisals and dyadic communication of both patients and spouses are associated with their quality of life.

the results of the study support the hypothesis that the patient’s appraisals of their illness are related to their QOL and that the patient’s and the partner’s appraisals are related to their dyadic communication.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
patients’ and spouses’ perceptions of their illness are associated with their QOL and that dyadic communication is a mediator of this relationship.
the appraisals of patients and spouses are associated with their long term QOL.
the more the patient and the spouse communicate about the illness and the more positive they perceive that communication to be, the better the QOL for each of them.
The main takeaway from our work is that
patients’ and spouses’ QOL is not just a product of their own experiences, but also a function of their partners’ experiences.
both patients and their spouses should be involved in the treatment and care of prostate cancer.
patients and spouses are not just separate actors in a relationship, but are also partners who influence each other’s appraisals and QOL.
